paper_b.title: A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting

metadata.description: Mason et al. (paper277) recast AdaBoost (paper270) as a special case of AnyBoost, a generic functional gradient-descent procedure on convex combinations of base hypotheses. The same AdaBoost algorithm is re-derived as coordinate descent on the exponential margin loss in function space, providing an alternative interpretation and proof technique (gradient descent / convergence in function space) for the original Freund-Schapire result. The pair fits the AP (alternative proof) relation: same algorithmic object, fundamentally different theoretical machinery (functional gradient vs. multiplicative-weights potential).

matches.explanation: Paper A explicitly cites AdaBoost (Freund & Schapire) as an external algorithm and recovers it as the AnyBoost specialization with margin cost c(z) = e^{-z} and line-search step size. Paper B's AP270.2 is the original AdaBoost definition. Same algorithm; A's node is the citation pointer, B's is the constructive definition.

AnyBoost (paper A's main algorithmic contribution) is a generic functional gradient-descent meta-algorithm of which AdaBoost is one instantiation. The two algorithms play parallel roles: AnyBoost is the gradient-descent reframing of which AdaBoost is the canonical example. Cross-paper, AnyBoost generalizes the per-round update of AdaBoost from multiplicative-weights to functional gradient steps; the weights D(i) in AdaBoost correspond to the gradient -c'(y_i F(x_i)) of the exponential margin cost (made explicit by paper A's EP277.3).

Paper A's EP277.3 shows that maximizing -<grad C(F), f> reduces to minimizing the weighted misclassification error sum_{i: f(x_i) != y_i} D(i) with weights D(i) ∝ -c'(y_i F(x_i)). This is precisely the role of step (3) in AdaBoost (paper B), where WeakLearn is called with distribution p^t and returns h_t minimizing weighted error ε_t. The correspondence D(i) ∝ exp(-y_i F_{t-1}(x_i)) (when c(z)=e^{-z}) is the bridge between the two frameworks.

Paper A's empirical inner product (DP277.4) and margin cost functional (DP277.5) play the role of B's cumulative-loss bookkeeping (DP270.1): both are the per-sample aggregation that defines what the boosting/online algorithm minimizes. Different formulations — A's is a function-space inner product on linear combinations of base hypotheses, B's is a sum of strategy losses — but both serve as the objective the iterative procedure descends on.

Paper A's weak learner oracle L(F) (returns f with large -<grad C(F), f>) corresponds to paper B's weak PAC-learning algorithm (returns h with error <= 1/2 - γ). Same conceptual role — produce a base hypothesis better than chance under a current weighting — but A frames it as functional-gradient maximization while B uses the PAC framework. Cross-type compatible (definition ↔ definition), with the formulations differing in what 'better than chance' means.

Paper B's TP270.6 is AdaBoost's training-error bound ε ≤ 2^T ∏ √(ε_t(1-ε_t)) — convergence of AdaBoost. Paper A's TP277.1 (AnyBoost convergence) and TP277.2 (global optimality at accumulation points) are the functional-gradient-descent analogues: under Lipschitz-differentiable cost and prescribed step size, AnyBoost drives the gradient inner product to zero (TP277.1) and reaches the global cost minimum under convexity + negation closure + exact weak learning (TP277.2). Different proof technique entirely (gradient descent in Banach space vs. potential-function/multiplicative-weights argument), and different conclusion form (asymptotic gradient → 0 vs. explicit finite-time exponential bound), so this is genuinely an alternative-proof correspondence rather than an identity.

Both papers target the same underlying problem: combine base hypotheses to minimize misclassification probability. Paper A states it as a function-space optimization (ProbP277.1: minimize C(F) over lin(F)) plus the downstream classification objective (ProbP277.2). Paper B states it directly as the boosting problem (ProbP270.2). A frames the problem in terms of a surrogate (margin) cost on lin(F); B frames it in PAC terms. Same problem, different formal wrapping.

ExP277.1 (Table 1 of paper A) is the unification example showing AdaBoost = AnyBoost with exponential cost + line search. The match with AP270.2 (AdaBoost) records that this example explicitly contains B's algorithm as a row in A's unification table. This is the single most direct piece of evidence that the two papers describe the same algorithm under different formalisms.

The inner-product function-space setup (DP277.1) and the pointwise functional gradient ∇C(F) (DP277.2) are paper A's central new objects — the machinery that lets boosting be re-read as gradient descent. Paper B has no analogue: AdaBoost in B is constructed and analyzed entirely with multiplicative weights and a potential-function (Σ w_i^{T+1}) argument, never invoking function-space inner products or functional derivatives.

EP277.1 (first-order expansion C(F+εf) = C(F) + ε<∇C(F), f>) and EP277.2 (closed form of -<∇C(F), f> for margin costs) are the functional-gradient algebra unique to A's reframing. B's analysis never linearises a cost in a function-space direction, so these have no counterpart.

The normalized sigmoid cost (DP277.6) and the DOOM II algorithm (AP277.2) are paper A's concrete contribution beyond mere unification: a non-AdaBoost member of the AnyBoost family explicitly designed to be more noise-robust. Paper B does not consider non-exponential margin costs.

All three are empirical experiments specific to paper A: DOOM II vs AdaBoost on UCI data with label noise (ExP277.2), margin distributions (ExP277.3), and the sigmoid-cost-predicts-AdaBoost-overfitting study (ExP277.4). Paper B contains no experiments and no comparable empirical material.

The entire on-line allocation / Hedge(β) chain (ProbP270.1, AP270.1, LP270.1, TP270.2, TP270.3, LP270.4, EP270.1, TP270.5, EP270.2) is paper B's general decision-theoretic framework, of which AdaBoost is one application. Paper A focuses purely on boosting and never engages with the on-line allocation problem, expert prediction, or the Hedge regret bound. These are entirely paper-B-specific contributions.

Paper B's VC-dimension bound on Θ_T(H) (TP270.8) — the class of T-fold linear thresholds of base hypotheses — is a generalisation-error result for AdaBoost. Paper A is a NIPS short paper that defers all generalisation-bound discussion to the cited [Mason, Bartlett, Baxter 1999] companion (see RP277.3); no analogue appears in A's JSON.

TP270.9 (soft-threshold AdaBoost bound) is a refinement of B's training-error bound by a factor 2 using a smoothed final hypothesis. Paper A does not consider soft-threshold variants of the final combined hypothesis.

AdaBoost.M1, AdaBoost.M2 (with pseudo-loss), and AdaBoost.R for regression — together with their training-error bounds and the oblivious-hypothesis example — are all multi-class / regression extensions of binary AdaBoost in paper B. Paper A confines itself to binary classification with the empirical L^2 inner product (DP277.4) and never addresses multi-class or regression boosting.
